title: "Troubleshooting"
subtitle: "Reading error messages, and fixing package installation problems on Windows and Mac"
---

This page has two parts: how to read an R error message and fix the most common ones, and how to fix packages that won't install.

## Reading error messages

Everyone who writes R gets error messages, every day. An error isn't a sign that you're doing badly: it's R telling you exactly where it got stuck. Session 1 showed the difference between an **error** (R stopped), a **warning** (R finished, but something may be wrong), and a **message** (just information).

### The parts of an error

Here is an error from Session 2, when a column name has a typo:

```
Error in `mutate()`:
ℹ In argument: `x = mean(agee)`.
Caused by error:
! object 'agee' not found
```

-   **`Error in mutate()`** — the function that stopped. Look for it in your code.
-   **`ℹ In argument:`** — the exact piece of code inside that function.
-   **`Caused by error:` / `!`** — the actual problem. Read this line first: there's no column or object called `agee`.
-   Lines starting with **`ℹ`** are hints, and **`✖`** lines say what went wrong. Tidyverse messages often suggest the fix.

### Five steps when you get an error

1.  **Read the last line first** (the one with `!`). It usually says what's wrong.
2.  **Find the function** named after `Error in`, and look at that line of your code.
3.  **Check the spelling** of every name: columns, objects, functions. R treats `Age` and `age` as different names.
4.  **Run the code piece by piece.** In a pipeline, select the lines up to just before a `%>%` and run them. Add one line at a time until the error appears.
5.  **Still stuck?** Search for the exact message in quotes (leave out your own object names), check the function's help page with `?function_name`, or ask: a person, or an [AI assistant](ai-assistants.qmd) (with care).

### Common errors in this workshop

| What R says | What it usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `object 'linelst' not found` | A typo in a name, or you never ran the line that creates it | Check the spelling; run the line with `<-` first |
| `could not find function "clean_names"` | The package isn't loaded | Run `library(janitor)` (each session starts with the `library()` lines) |
| `could not find function "%>%"` | The tidyverse isn't loaded | Run `library(tidyverse)` |
| `there is no package called ‘tidyvers’` | A typo, or the package isn't installed | Check the spelling, or run `install.packages("tidyverse")` once |
| `No such file: .../raw_data/linelist.xlsx` | The file name or folder is wrong, or Positron didn't open the workshop folder | Check the name in the **Explorer**; open the folder with **File → Open Folder...** |
| `Can't select columns that don't exist.` ``✖ Column `Age` doesn't exist.`` | A column name is misspelled | Check with `names(DATA)`; after `clean_names()` names are lower case |
| `We detected a named input.` ``ℹ Did you mean `age_years == 5`?`` | `=` instead of `==` in `filter()` | Use `==` to compare, `=` only to name things |
| `unexpected ')'` or `unexpected numeric constant` | A bracket too many, or a missing comma | Count the brackets; put a comma between arguments |
| `non-numeric argument to binary operator` | Maths on text, for example `"38" + 1` | Convert with `as.numeric()` (Session 2) |
| `` `mapping` must be created by `aes()`. `` R then asks whether you used `%>%` instead of `+` | `%>%` between ggplot layers | Join ggplot layers with `+` |
| `` Cannot use `+` with a single argument `` | A `+` at the start of a line in a ggplot | Put `+` at the **end** of the line before |
| The Console shows `+` and waits | The command isn't finished: an open bracket or quote, or a `%>%` at the end of the last line | Press **Esc**, then fix the code |

And one **warning** you'll see often: `NAs introduced by coercion` means `as.numeric()` met text it couldn't turn into a number (like "unknown") and made it `NA`. That's often what you want, but check how many `NA`s you got.

::: callout-tip
## No error doesn't mean right

Code can run without an error and still give a wrong answer: a misspelled category in `case_when()` or `filter()` silently matches nothing. Check results with `count()` and `summary()` after each step (Sessions 2, 3, and 8 show examples).
:::

## Installing packages

Some R packages have to be compiled when you install them. If `install.packages()` fails with errors about compilers, `make`, `gfortran`, or missing files like `cmath`, follow the steps for your computer below.


### Windows users – installing Rtools (required for compiling R packages)

Some R packages are available only as source code. On Windows you need
Rtools (a collection of compilers and build utilities) so that R can
install those packages. macOS and Linux already ship suitable build
tools; Windows does not.

1)  Do I already have Rtools?

In a fresh R session (the Positron Console) run:

```r
Sys.which("make")
```

-   If you get a blank result (""), R cannot find make ⇒ Rtools is
    missing. • If you see a full path containing
    rtools…\usr\bin\make.exe, you’re all set! NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!

2)  Find the Rtools version that matches your R

Check your R version:

```r
R.version.string
```

-   Your R version Install this Rtools 4.5.x Rtools45 4.4.x Rtools44
    4.3.x Rtools43 4.2.x Rtools42 (no longer needed if you upgraded R)

3)  Download Rtools

-   Go to <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/> Click the
    folder for your version (e.g. rtools43 for 4.3; rtools44 for 4.4;
    rtools45 for 4.5). Download the .exe installer (≈ 200 MB).

4)  Install Rtools

-   Close Positron (or RStudio). Run the downloaded installer. When prompted, tick
    “Add Rtools to system PATH.” Accept the default install path
    (C:\rtools45, C:\rtools44, …). Finish the installation (it may take
    a minute).

5)  Verify the installation

-   After installation open a new R session (or reboot) and run:

```r
Sys.which("make")
#>                  make 
#> "C:\\rtools45\\usr\\bin\\make.exe"   # or rtools44 / rtools43
```

---

### Mac users – installing gfortran and Xcode Command Line Tools (required for compiling R packages)

-   macOS users – installing gfortran (required for compiling R
    packages)

-   Some R packages require a Fortran compiler to install from source.

-   macOS does not include one by default.

-   You need to install gfortran manually and the version must match
    your R version.

1.  Do I already have gfortran?

In a fresh R session (the Positron Console) run:

```r
Sys.which("gfortran") 
```

-   If you get a blank result (""), gfortran is missing ⇒ you need to
    install it.

-   If you see a path like /opt/gfortran/bin/gfortran, you're all set!
    NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!

2.  Find the gfortran version that matches your R Check your R version:

-   Look at the top of the R console window OR

-   copy/paste this into your terminal

```
R.version.string 
```

-   If your R version is 4.5.x Install gfortran

-   If your R version is 4.3 to 4.4.x install gfortran 12.2

-   If you R version is older then no need to install gfortran

3.  Download gfortran

-   <https://mac.r-project.org/tools/gfortran-12.2-universal.pkg>

-   <https://mac.r-project.org/tools/gfortran-14.2-universal.pkg>

4.  Install gfortran

-   Close Positron (or RStudio).

-   Double-click the downloaded .pkg file.

-   Follow the installer prompts and accept the default install path.
    Enter your Mac password when prompted. Finish the installation.

5.  Verify the installation After installation open a new R session
    and run:

```
Sys.which("gfortran") 
#\> gfortran 
#\> "/opt/gfortran/bin/gfortran" 
```

-   If you see the path above, gfortran is installed correctly ✅

-   If you still get a blank result, try restarting your Mac and running
    again.

6.  One more check - verify R and gfortran are in sync

-   Run this in R:

```
system("gfortran --version") 
```

You should see output like:

```
GNU Fortran (GCC) 14.2.0 # if you are on R 4.5 
GNU Fortran (GCC) 12.2.0 # if you are on R 4.4 or 4.3 
```

-   If the version number does not match your R version, you have the
    wrong gfortran installed and need to download the correct version
    from <https://mac.r-project.org/tools/>

-   macOS users – fixing missing C++ header files (required for
    compiling R packages)

If you see errors like these when installing packages:

```
fatal error: 'cmath' file not found 
fatal error: 'cstdlib' file not 
found fatal error: 'cstring' file not found 
```

This means your Xcode Command Line Tools are missing or out of date.
This is common after a macOS upgrade.

a.  Do I have this problem?

In R run:

```
system("xcode-select -p")
```

-   If you get an error or a blank result ⇒ Command Line Tools are
    missing. • If you see /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools ⇒ they are
    installed. NO NEED TO GO ANY FURTHER!

b.  Fix the problem Close Positron (or RStudio) completely. Open the Mac
    Terminal application and run these commands one at a time:

#### Step 1 - Remove the old Command Line Tools:

```bash
sudo rm -rf /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools 
```

-   You will be prompted for your Mac password.
-   Type it and press Enter (you will not see the password as you type -
    this is normal).

#### Step 2 - Reinstall the Command Line Tools:

```bash
xcode-select --install 
```

-   A popup window will appear.
-   Click Install and wait for it to finish.
-   **This may take 5 to 10 minutes depending on your internet
    connection**

#### Step 3 - Verify the installation was successful:

```bash
xcode-select -p 
```

-   You should see:

```
/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools
```

a.  Try installing your packages again

-   Once the Command Line Tools are installed, reopen Positron and re-run
    the `install.packages()` line in Part 2 of the Session 1 student
    script.

#### ⚠️ Note for macOS beta users:

If you are running a beta version of macOS, package compilation errors
are more likely because R and its tools may not yet be fully compatible
with the newest macOS releases. If you continue to have problems after
reinstalling the Command Line Tools, the most reliable solution is to
use the stable (non-beta) release of macOS.
